tip: The video and audio a camera or phone recorded, before it is edited.
meaning: Footage is everything the camera recorded. It is the raw material you cut, like flour before you bake a cake.
example: You film your dog for ten minutes at the park. Those ten minutes are your footage.
vukem: Footage is what you [import into the media library](/docs/guide/media-library). Each file becomes an asset.

tip: Footage straight from the camera, with nothing cut or changed yet.
meaning: Raw footage is video nobody has touched. It still has the mistakes, the waiting and the parts you will throw away.
example: Before your birthday video is cut, the clip with everyone saying "ready, set..." three times is raw footage.

tip: One piece of video that was filmed without stopping the camera.
meaning: A shot starts when the camera starts and ends when the camera stops (or when you cut away). A video is many shots in a row.
example: Zooming slowly on a birthday cake until the candles fill the screen is one shot.

tip: One try at filming a shot.
meaning: When a shot goes wrong, you film it again. Each try is a take, usually counted "take one, take two...".
example: Your friend laughs in the middle of saying a line, so you do take two.

tip: A part of a story in one place and one time, made of several shots.
meaning: A scene is a piece of the story that happens in one place at one time. It is usually built from several shots.
example: Everything that happens in the kitchen while you bake is one scene, filmed in many shots.

tip: One single still picture of a video.
meaning: A video is a very fast flip-book. Each page of the flip-book is a frame. Show enough of them each second and the pictures seem to move.
example: A phone video at 30 frames per second has 30 pictures for every second you watch.
vukem: Vukem Video counts time in frames, and you can write a position as `97f`. See [Time](/docs/concepts/time).

tip: How many pictures a video shows each second, written as fps.
meaning: The frame rate is the number of frames shown in one second. More frames make motion look smoother. Cinema uses 24, many phones use 30 or 60.
example: Slow-motion looks smooth because the camera filmed 120 frames each second and the video plays them at 30.
vukem: A new project is 30 fps by default; `settings.set_fps` changes it. See [Projects](/docs/projects).

tip: The shape of the picture: how wide it is compared with how tall it is.
meaning: The aspect ratio is width and height written as two numbers, like 16:9. A big first number means wide, like a TV. A big second number means tall, like a phone held upright.
example: A YouTube video is usually 16:9 (wide). A TikTok is 9:16 (tall).
vukem: The presets are 9:16 (the default), 16:9, 1:1 and 4:5. `settings.reframe` changes it. See [Projects](/docs/projects).

tip: How many tiny dots (pixels) make up the picture, wide by tall.
meaning: Resolution counts the pixels in the picture, like 1920 by 1080. More pixels mean more detail, and a bigger file.
example: A photo printed very large looks blurry if it has too few pixels.

tip: The smallest dot of a picture; millions of them make an image.
meaning: A pixel is one tiny coloured square. Your screen is a grid of them, and each shows one colour.
example: Zoom a photo until it looks like blocks. Each block is a pixel.

tip: From where, and how high or low, the camera looks at the subject.
meaning: The angle is where you put the camera. Looking up at someone makes them seem big and strong. Looking down makes them seem small.
example: Filming a puppy from the floor makes the puppy look like a hero.

tip: A tilted camera so the horizon is slanted on purpose.
meaning: Tilt the camera sideways and everything looks crooked. Filmmakers do it to make you feel nervous or dizzy.
example: In a scary movie, the picture tilts when the monster walks in.

tip: A shot that shows the whole place, with people looking small.
meaning: A wide shot is far away. You see the person and the place around them, like a whole football field.
example: A wide shot of a kid on a huge empty beach shows how alone they are.

tip: A shot that shows a person from about the waist up.
meaning: A medium shot is in between: close enough to see the face and hands, far enough to see a bit of the room.
example: Someone telling a story at the dinner table is usually filmed in a medium shot.

tip: A shot so near that a face or one object fills the screen.
meaning: A close-up shows one small thing very big, like a face, a hand or an eye. It tells the audience: look at this.
example: A close-up of a hand reaching for the last cookie.

tip: A wide shot at the start that tells where the story is.
meaning: An establishing shot shows the place first, so the viewer knows where they are before the people appear.
example: A picture of a school building, then a cut to the classroom inside.

tip: A shot taken from behind one person, looking at the other.
meaning: You see the back of one person's head and shoulder, and the face of the person they are talking to.
example: Two friends talking: the camera sits behind one friend and looks at the other.

tip: A shot that shows what a character sees, as if through their eyes.
meaning: In a point-of-view shot the camera is the character's eyes. The viewer sees exactly what they see.
example: A video from a bike helmet camera, showing the road ahead.

tip: A close shot of a small detail, added to show something important.
meaning: An insert shot shows one small thing the story needs, like a clock, a note or a button.
example: A close shot of the note that says "Meet me at 5".

tip: Turning the camera left or right without moving it from its place.
meaning: To pan, you stay still and swing the camera sideways, like turning your head to follow a car passing by.
example: Panning slowly across the whole class photo, from the first kid to the last.

tip: Pointing the camera up or down without moving it from its place.
meaning: A tilt is a pan's cousin: the camera nods up or down instead of turning sideways.
example: Tilting up from a skater's shoes to their face.

tip: A shot where the camera itself travels along with the subject.
meaning: In a tracking shot the camera moves, on wheels or on a person's feet, and follows the action.
example: Walking backwards with a phone while your friend runs toward you.

tip: Changing the lens so the subject looks closer or farther away.
meaning: A zoom makes things look nearer without you moving. Careful: the picture also gets blurrier on a phone, because it just stretches pixels.
example: Zooming in on the birthday candles from across the room.

tip: A number that says how wide or how zoomed-in a lens sees.
meaning: A small focal length (like 14 mm) sees a wide view. A big one (like 200 mm) sees a narrow, far-away view.
example: A phone's "wide" camera has a smaller focal length than its "telephoto" camera.

tip: How much of the picture, near to far, is sharp.
meaning: With a shallow depth of field only the thing you focus on is sharp and the background is soft and blurry. With a deep one, everything is sharp.
example: A portrait where the person is sharp and the trees behind are a soft blur.

tip: How wide the lens opens to let light in.
meaning: The aperture is a hole in the lens that gets wider or narrower, like the pupil of your eye. A wider hole lets in more light and makes the background blurrier.
example: In a dark room the camera opens its aperture wide to get enough light.

tip: How much light the camera lets in, so the picture is dark or bright.
meaning: Exposure is the amount of light that reaches the camera. Too little and the picture is too dark. Too much and it turns white.
example: Filming a friend in front of a bright window turns them into a dark shape: the exposure is for the window.

tip: A camera setting that makes the picture brighter, but also grainier.
meaning: A high ISO makes the camera more sensitive to light, so dark scenes look brighter. The price is noise: little coloured speckles.
example: A phone video at night looks grainy because the camera turned the ISO way up.

tip: How long the camera looks at each frame; short is crisp, long is blurry.
meaning: A fast shutter freezes motion. A slow shutter leaves a smear. For video, a common rule is to use about double the frame rate (1/48 s for 24 fps).
example: A short shutter freezes the water drops of a splash. A long one makes them a smooth veil.

tip: Making the thing you care about sharp, not blurry.
meaning: When something is in focus its edges are clear. Cameras can focus by themselves (autofocus) or you can turn a ring by hand.
example: The picture starts blurry and becomes sharp when the camera finds the face.

tip: Changing the focus during a shot, so attention moves from one thing to another.
meaning: You start with the near object sharp and the far one blurry, then you change the focus so the far one becomes sharp.
example: The flower in front is sharp. The focus slides and now the girl behind it is sharp.

tip: Filming while holding the camera, which makes the picture wobble a little.
meaning: Handheld footage is shot without a stand, so it shakes a bit. It feels real and close, but can make people dizzy if it shakes too much.
example: A video you film by walking and holding your phone.

tip: A three-legged stand that holds the camera still.
meaning: A tripod keeps the camera steady so the picture does not wobble. Many shots look better on one.
example: Filming a time-lapse of the sunset: you put the camera on a tripod and leave it.

tip: A holder with motors that keeps the camera smooth while you walk.
meaning: A gimbal tilts and turns by itself to cancel your shaking, so you can walk and still get a smooth shot.
example: Walking through a crowd with a phone on a gimbal and no wobble.

tip: Making a shaky video smooth, by the camera or by software.
meaning: Stabilization removes shaking. Some cameras do it while filming. Editors can do it afterwards by moving and cropping each frame a little.
example: A bike video that was bumpy looks smoother after stabilization, but a bit more zoomed-in.

tip: Video played slower than real life, so movement looks stretched out.
meaning: Film many frames each second (like 120) and play them at a normal speed (like 30): everything looks four times slower.
example: A balloon popping, shown slowly so you see the rubber tear.

tip: Many pictures taken far apart in time and played fast, so hours become seconds.
meaning: A time-lapse takes one picture every few seconds or minutes. When you play them quickly, slow things like clouds seem to rush.
example: A flower opening in ten seconds when it really took a whole day.

tip: Video filmed or made tall, like a phone held upright.
meaning: Vertical video is taller than wide, usually 9:16. It fills a phone screen, so apps like TikTok and Reels use it.
example: A video you film holding the phone upright and watch without turning the phone.
vukem: 9:16 is the default frame of a Vukem Video project.

tip: A small board filmed at the start of a take with its name and number.
meaning: The slate (or clapperboard) shows the scene and take number. It is filmed first so that, later, the editor can tell the takes apart.
example: Someone holds a board, says "scene 4, take 2" and snaps the clapper.

tip: Tiny random speckles in the picture, common in dark scenes.
meaning: In a dark scene the camera boosts the signal and also boosts its own mistakes. You see them as colourful sand on the picture.
example: A phone video filmed at night looks like it is covered with sand.

tip: The glass in front of the camera that gathers light and shapes the picture.
meaning: The lens decides how wide the view is and how blurry the background is. A phone has several tiny lenses.
example: Switching from the 1x to the 0.5x camera on a phone changes the lens.

tip: The chip in the camera that turns light into the picture.
meaning: The sensor is a grid of tiny light detectors. A bigger sensor catches more light, so pictures are cleaner in the dark.
example: A big camera filmed the dark party better than a small phone because its sensor is bigger.
